claims.evidence: Search summaries: HbA1c reflects average glucose over roughly 2-3 months; used to diagnose type 2 diabetes and monitor people with diabetes.
Reflects average blood glucose over the previous 2 to 3 months (8-12 weeks).
Lab Tests Online UK: HbA1c covers a longer window; a fingerstick reading is a single snapshot.
Plain, undisputed physiology (glucose binds haemoglobin in red cells); not stated in the returned text.
Red blood cells live about 8-12 weeks before being replaced, so the test covers the previous 8-12 weeks.
No retrieved text says occasional extremes are smoothed; sources say only that it does not capture short-term spikes or dips.
claims.newSentence: Because it covers a longer window, the test does not show short-term rises or dips in glucose.

claims.evidence: Main blood test used to diagnose type 2 diabetes.
Used to screen people at high risk; a result in the intermediate band indicates high risk and is usually followed by lifestyle advice and monitoring.
Shows how well glucose has been controlled over the previous 8-12 weeks in people with diabetes.
HbA1c test is not used for diagnosing type 1 diabetes or diabetes during pregnancy.
Nothing retrieved on home glucose monitors. Sources say HbA1c is the usual first-line blood test for diagnosing type 2 diabetes.
claims.newSentence: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with blood tests, and HbA1c is the usual first test.

claims.evidence: Results appear in mmol/mol or as a percentage; HbA1c used to be given as a percentage; UK reports in mmol/mol.
Retrieved text supports an individualised target agreed with the person but attributes it to NICE-based guidance, not Diabetes UK.
claims.newSentence: NICE-based guidance says an individual HbA1c target should be agreed with each person.

claims.evidence: Targets relaxed where tight control risks hypoglycaemia.
Targets may be relaxed for older or frail people or where tight control risks hypoglycaemia.
Three-to-six-month interval was attributed by the text to NICE, not Diabetes UK (which says entitled to at least a yearly test).
claims.newSentence: NICE patient information advises that HbA1c is usually tested every three to six months.

claims.evidence: Only 'more often if glucose is changing quickly' was seen; pregnancy planning and treatment change not returned.
claims.newSentence: It may be done more often if blood glucose levels are changing quickly.

claims.evidence: No source said some people need testing less often in pregnancy; NICE text says every 6 months once stable.
claims.newSentence: Once blood glucose is stable, NICE patient information says the test is usually every six months.

claims.evidence: Accuracy affected by conditions affecting red blood cells such as haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia; variants interfere.
Advice to talk to doctor not seen. Guidance says glucose-based tests are used when HbA1c is unreliable.
claims.newSentence: Where HbA1c is unreliable, glucose-based blood tests are used for diagnosis instead.

claims.evidence: Pregnancy, transfusion, heavy bleeding listed; illness not seen.
claims.newSentence: Pregnancy, heavy bleeding and recent blood transfusion can also make HbA1c unreliable.

claims.evidence: HbA1c may change if diet, physical activity, weight or medication have changed.
Laboratories 'often' converting not stated; eAG converts HbA1c to meter units but is an average, not an exact match.
claims.newSentence: An estimated average glucose converts HbA1c into meter units, but it is an average and not an exact match for readings.

claims.evidence: Scottish guidance on GP explaining risk factors not seen. England consensus: intermediate result usually leads to lifestyle advice.
claims.newSentence: The usual response to an intermediate result is lifestyle advice on eating, activity and weight.

claims.evidence: Returned text: GP can refer, many areas allow self-referral, eligibility varies; 'should refer' not stated.
claims.newSentence: A GP can refer eligible people to the free NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme, and some areas allow self-referral.

claims.evidence: No national rule of yearly test for all; England consensus says intermediate result is monitored at least yearly.
claims.newSentence: People with an intermediate result are usually monitored at least once a year.

claims.evidence: Signposting; plain and undisputed.
HbA1c in the intermediate band indicates prediabetes / high risk rather than diabetes.
Intermediate result signals high risk of developing diabetes.
Prediabetes usually causes no symptoms and is found with blood tests; NHS Health Check not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: Prediabetes usually causes no symptoms, so it is found through blood tests.

claims.evidence: NHS diabetes page lists thirst, urinating more, tiredness and unintended weight loss as common signs.
Advice to see a GP not seen; NHS notes not everyone has symptoms and checking matters.
claims.newSentence: The NHS notes that not everyone with diabetes has symptoms, which is why getting checked matters.

claims.evidence: Programme is free, nine months, support with eating, activity and weight; referral route varies.
claims.newSentence: The programme is free, lasts nine months and gives support with healthy eating, physical activity and weight.

claims.evidence: Average glucose over previous 2-3 months.
Used to diagnose, monitor, and screen people at high risk.
Targets individualised; relaxed for older/frail or hypo-prone people.
Conditions affecting red cells make HbA1c unreliable; alternative tests used.

additions.sentence: A raised result in someone without symptoms is usually repeated, and a second result in the diabetes range confirms the diagnosis.
additions.evidence: If asymptomatic, repeat venous HbA1c; still in diabetes range confirms diagnosis.

additions.sentence: HbA1c is not used to diagnose diabetes during pregnancy.
additions.evidence: HbA1c test is not used for diagnosing diabetes during pregnancy or type 1 diabetes.

additions.sentence: One hospital guideline says HbA1c should not be used for diagnosis when symptoms have appeared over less than a month.
additions.evidence: With a short history (<1 month) of thirst, urinary frequency or weight loss, HbA1c should NOT be used as a diagnostic test.

additions.sentence: Heavy bleeding or haemolytic anaemia can make HbA1c falsely low, while iron deficiency may raise it.
additions.evidence: Haemolytic anaemia or heavy bleeding may give falsely low results; iron deficiency may raise HbA1c.

additions.sentence: Some haemoglobin variants can interfere with HbA1c measurement, so other methods may be needed.
additions.evidence: Some haemoglobin variants can interfere with HbA1c measurement and alternative methods may be required.

additions.sentence: Eligibility for the Diabetes Prevention Programme varies by area, so the local service sets the rules.
additions.evidence: One London ICB requires a result within 24 months, another within 12 months; check local service.

notes: Search summaries blended pages; 'supported' means the returned summary text stated it. Diabetes UK page text not shown directly, claims attributed to it were rechecked via NICE/Devon/Lab Tests Online wording. Interval and target figures in edits are NICE-attributed; consider removing numbers if house style prefers.
